reconcile.connective: Defenders read Genesis 2:19's verb as a pluperfect — God had already formed the animals on day six and now brings them to Adam — so the two accounts state one sequence, not two.

discrepancy.connective: Julius Wellhausen pressed the sharpest form of the objection: Genesis 1 (P) and Genesis 2 (J) are independent documents, and in J the man is formed before the animals, an order that cannot be folded into P's animals-then-humans sequence without dissolving one source into the other.

skeptic.name: Julius Wellhausen
skeptic.work: Prolegomena to the History of Israel
skeptic.attribution: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (Eng. trans. 1885; German Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels, 1883)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The circumstance that in Gen 2:19 the formation of the beasts and birds is connected with the creation of Adam by the imperf. c. ו consec., constitutes to objection to the plan of creation given in Gen 1. … so that our modern style of expressing the same thought would be simply this: "God brought to Adam the beasts which He had formed."
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: K&D names the exact grammatical hook critics use (the waw-consecutive 'and God formed' in 2:19) and answers it: it is no objection to Gen 1's order, because the verb means God brought animals He had already formed — the pluperfect/retrospective reading that harmonizes the two sequences. This is the single strongest on-tension harmonization on the row.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament, on Genesis 2:18-19 (1861-75)
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: Keil & Delitzsch treat this passage directly, arguing the waw-consecutive in Gen 2:19 raises no objection to Gen 1's order and is best read as 'God brought to Adam the beasts which He had formed' — the canonical pluperfect harmonization of the creation sequence.
